name: Metformin

lead: Metformin is a first-line type 2 diabetes drug. Some people use it off-label to cut belly fat, handle carbs better, calm acne and slow aging, and to manage blood sugar during testosterone or growth hormone use.

It lowers liver glucose output and improves insulin sensitivity, partly through AMPK activation, which is the chain toward less fat storage and possibly clearer skin. It has decades of safety data in diabetes, and observational studies in diabetics link it to lower cancer risk and mortality. Reviews in 2021 and 2025 take a cautious view of its effect on aging in people without diabetes, and some evidence suggests it may blunt exercise adaptations.

paras: Taken as a daily tablet with meals under a prescription, often ramped up gradually to limit digestive effects. Forum users discuss it for body composition and alongside hormone therapy, sometimes sourcing it from overseas pharmacies.

Common side effects are digestive upset, and vitamin B12 deficiency can develop with long-term use; rare lactic acidosis occurs mainly with kidney impairment. It may blunt muscle growth and endurance gains. Prescription-only in the US, UK and EU; off-label use for aging is not approved.

chain: Less belly fat, possibly clearer skin
angle.text: Metformin lowers glucose and insulin, which users link to better carb handling, less belly fat and possibly clearer skin. It is established for diabetes; appearance uses have been studied lightly, and some report it may blunt muscle growth.

lead: Metformin, sold under the brand name Glucophage among others, is a biguanide medication taken by mouth and the main first-line drug for type 2 diabetes, particularly in people who are overweight.[1] In appearance-focused communities it is discussed for its metabolic effects: it lowers blood glucose and insulin, is associated with modest weight and waist reductions in trials, and in PCOS has been studied for hirsutism and body composition, so people interested in leaner physiques, belly fat and insulin sensitivity ask about it.[1][2] It is also discussed in longevity circles as a candidate ageing-related drug, and some members of strength and hormone forums mention it alongside testosterone or growth hormone use.[3][4][5][6]

Metformin was first described in the scientific literature in 1922 by Emil Werner and James Bell, tested in humans for diabetes by the French physician Jean Sterne in 1957 and introduced in France that year; the US FDA approved it in 1994.[1] It is on the WHO List of Essential Medicines and in 2023 was the third most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with more than 82 million prescriptions.[1] It is also used in polycystic ovary syndrome (which Wikipedia terms polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome) and sometimes off-label to limit weight gain from antipsychotic drugs.[1]

Research relevant to the appearance community comes in several strands. The Diabetes Prevention Program reported lower diabetes incidence and small weight and waist reductions with metformin.[7][2] Studies in older adults have found that metformin blunted some adaptations to aerobic exercise and the muscle-size gain from resistance training, a finding often raised in bodybuilding forums.[2] Observational studies in diabetics, laboratory work on AMPK and mTOR signalling, and the planned TAME trial have made it a subject of ageing research, where reviews published in 2021 and 2025 take a cautious view of the evidence.[3][8][9][2] Metformin is prescription-only in the US, UK and EU.[1]

paras: The American Diabetes Association and the American College of Physicians recommend metformin as a first-line agent for type 2 diabetes, and it is as effective as repaglinide and more effective than other oral drugs according to Wikipedia.[1] A 2020 Annals of Internal Medicine network meta-analysis compared benefits and harms of glucose-lowering drugs.[10] The UKPDS 34 trial reported that intensive blood-glucose control with metformin affected complications in overweight patients with type 2 diabetes,[11] and a 10-year follow-up of intensive glucose control was published in 2008.[12] A 2006 trial compared the durability of glycaemic control with rosiglitazone, metformin and glyburide.[13]

In prediabetes, the Diabetes Prevention Program found in 2002 that lifestyle intervention or metformin reduced the incidence of type 2 diabetes,[7] and a 10-year follow-up reported on diabetes incidence and weight loss.[14] A 2019 systematic review summarised by Wikipedia found moderate-quality evidence that metformin reduced diabetes risk compared with placebo or usual diet and exercise, but not compared with intensive diet or exercise.[1]

subs.h: Polycystic ovary syndrome and other uses
paras: Wikipedia describes tentative evidence that metformin raises live birth rates in PCOS, including women who did not conceive with clomiphene.[1] A 2024 meta-analysis compared metformin with combined oral contraceptive pills,[15] 2023 and 2024 meta-analyses evaluated inositol as an alternative,[16][17] and a 2019 meta-analysis compared GLP-1 receptor agonists with metformin in PCOS.[18] Metformin has also been compared with insulin in gestational diabetes in a 2008 New England Journal of Medicine trial and a 2021 randomised trial,[19][20] and Wikipedia notes good short-term safety but unclear long-term safety for mother and child.[1] It is associated with weight loss in obesity without diabetes and with counteracting weight gain from olanzapine and clozapine.[1]

Metformin is not approved for weight loss, but its weight effects are documented. Wikipedia says it is typically associated with weight loss, and it counteracts weight gain from olanzapine and clozapine.[1] In the Diabetes Prevention Program, weight fell 2.06 percent with metformin versus 0.02 percent with placebo over the double-blind phase, and waist circumference fell 2.13 cm versus 0.79 cm; weight loss persisted in the open-label follow-up.[2] A 2019 analysis of the follow-up study found that participants who lost at least 5 percent of weight in year 1 and stayed on metformin kept off 6.2 percent over years 6 to 15, compared with 2.8 percent on placebo and 3.7 percent with lifestyle intervention.[2]

Smaller trials have measured body composition. A 1998 study by Lee and Morley reported lower calorie intake and hunger ratings after metformin in obese women with type 2 diabetes, and about 8 kg more maximum weight loss than placebo in women on a 1,200-calorie diet.[2] A randomised trial in obese women with PCOS by Pasquali and colleagues found that metformin added to a low-calorie diet reduced weight, BMI and visceral fat and improved hirsutism more than placebo.[2] In children with obesity and insulin resistance, a 2011 trial of 100 children reported greater reductions in BMI, weight and fat mass with metformin, with gastrointestinal effects limiting the dose in 17 percent.[2]

In PCOS, the hormonal condition that can bring acne, excess hair growth and weight gain, metformin has been compared with oral contraceptives, inositol and GLP-1 receptor agonists in meta-analyses.[15][16][17][18] Some guidelines do not recommend it first-line, according to Wikipedia.[1]

A question frequently raised among lifters is whether metformin affects training results. In a 2019 double-blind trial by Konopka and colleagues, adults around age 62 took placebo (n=26) or metformin (n=27) during 12 weeks of aerobic exercise training; metformin blunted gains in whole-body insulin sensitivity and VO2max and abolished the exercise-related rise in muscle mitochondrial respiration.[2]

The MASTERS trial by Walton and colleagues, also published in 2019, randomised adults aged 65 and older to metformin (n=46) or placebo (n=48) during 14 weeks of supervised resistance training. The placebo group gained more lean body mass and thigh muscle mass, with strength gains not significantly different; metformin raised AMPK signalling with a trend towards lower mTORC1 signalling.[2] Both trials enrolled older adults rather than young lifters. Wikipedia notes metformin has been called an exercise mimetic because it acts on AMPK and GLUT4, and that hypoglycaemia can occur with intense exercise or calorie restriction.[1]

Interest in metformin as an ageing-related drug stems from several lines of work. A 2005 BMJ study reported reduced cancer risk in diabetic patients taking it.[21] A 2013 study in Nature Communications by Martin-Montalvo and colleagues found that male mice given metformin in their diet from middle age had extended healthspan and lifespan at a low dietary concentration, while a tenfold higher concentration was toxic.[2] A 2014 UK database study by Bannister and colleagues reported that people with type 2 diabetes on metformin monotherapy (n=78,241) had survival that was not worse than matched non-diabetic controls (n=90,463), a result widely shared in longevity circles; commenters on Hacker News later noted that it had not been replicated, and observational comparisons of this type are open to confounding.[2][6]

In 2016, Barzilai, Crandall, Kritchevsky and Espeland argued in Cell Metabolism that metformin should be tested against ageing itself and described the planned Targeting Aging with Metformin (TAME) trial.[2] A 2020 Cell Metabolism review argues metformin attenuates several hallmarks of ageing,[3] whereas a 2021 critical review in Frontiers in Endocrinology examined whether the evidence supports it as an anti-ageing drug,[9] and a 2025 review in Ageing Research Reviews describes emerging uncertainty about its anti-ageing potential.[8] A large randomised trial of metformin in about 3,000 people aged 65 to 79 without glucose intolerance was described as ongoing in a 2024 review. A 2024 Hacker News thread on a Cell study reporting slower ageing markers in aged male monkeys drew discussion about mTORC1, AMPK and appetite effects and about whether results translate to people.[6]
Hacker News carried a 2019 CNBC headline on metformin for cancer prevention and longevity being popular in Silicon Valley, with commenters sceptical.[6]

Metformin lowers blood glucose by decreasing glucose production in the liver, increasing insulin sensitivity in tissues, and, according to Wikipedia, raising secretion of GDF15, which reduces appetite.[1] A 2001 study identified activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) as part of its mechanism,[22] an enzyme that senses energy status and interacts with NAD+ metabolism and SIRT1 activity.[23] A 2000 paper provided evidence that metformin inhibits complex 1 of the mitochondrial respiratory chain,[24] and Grokipedia also lists effects on intestinal glucose absorption and the gut microbiome.[25] A randomised trial reported that metformin changes gut microbiome composition and circulating short-chain fatty acids.[26] mTOR and HIF-1alpha signalling are involved in the metabolic basis of trained immunity in a 2014 Science paper listed among metformin literature.[27]

The most common adverse effects are gastrointestinal: diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, cramps and flatulence, most frequent when starting or increasing the dose. Wikipedia says about 5 percent of people cannot tolerate it even at low doses and that slow or extended-release preparations can improve tolerability.[1] Reviews describe how metformin acts on the gastrointestinal tract and how intolerance may be overcome.[28][29]

Long-term use is associated with lower vitamin B12 and higher homocysteine, and some researchers recommend screening; the Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study reported a link between long-term metformin use and B12 deficiency.[1][30] Lactic acidosis is rare and linked to impaired liver or kidney function; the US label carries a boxed warning, and Wikipedia states the FDA recommends avoiding metformin at eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2.[1][31] Metformin carries a small risk of hypoglycaemia, usually with intense exercise, calorie deficit or other glucose-lowering drugs.[1] Contraindications include severe renal impairment, hypersensitivity and metabolic acidosis.[1] Pregnancy data have not linked metformin to a clear increase in major birth defects.[31]

Well-powered randomised trials establish metformin's role in glycaemic control, prediabetes and pregnancy-related uses; see the Diabetes Prevention Program,[7] UKPDS 34,[11] and the metformin versus insulin gestational diabetes trial.[19] Trials of combination therapy include metformin with atorvastatin in diabetes and dyslipidaemia (ATOMIC)[32] and initial combination of empagliflozin and metformin.[33]

In ageing, the available human evidence is mainly observational data from diabetics and small mechanistic studies, and reviews published in 2021 and 2025 describe the case for a lifespan or healthspan benefit as uncertain.[8][9] A randomised trial in cancer survivors who were overweight or obese examined effects of metformin and behavioural weight loss on the gut microbiome.[26] Registered studies include metformin for insulin resistance in hepatitis C (n=126),[34] a trial of metformin plus clomiphene for ovulation induction in insulin-resistant PCOS (n=388, terminated),[35] and a study in obesity,[36] along with numerous bioequivalence studies.[37]

Controlled trials of metformin on body-composition outcomes exist in diabetes, prediabetes, PCOS and childhood obesity,[2] but no clinical study was found testing metformin for facial, skin or hair appearance outcomes in people without a metabolic indication.

Metformin derives from guanidine compounds found in the plant Galega officinalis (goat's rue), long used in herbal medicine for diabetes-like symptoms. It was synthesised in the 1920s, set aside after insulin became available, re-evaluated in the 1940s and brought into clinical use in France in 1957 after Jean Sterne's work.[1][25] The FDA approved it in 1994 according to Grokipedia.[25] The UKPDS results in 1998 gave major support to its use in overweight type 2 diabetes,[11] and the Diabetes Prevention Program in 2002 supported its use in prediabetes.[7]

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: On T Nation, members mention metformin in several roles. Some describe taking it after a type 2 diabetes diagnosis and ask how its insulin-sensitising effect relates to muscle gain,[38][39] others report using it alongside testosterone replacement therapy and say their carbohydrate sensitivity improved,[40] a physician reportedly agreed it might help belly fat during TRT,[41] and a post in a growth-hormone discussion describes using it to manage blood sugar.[4] One member said he had read on the forum that metformin inhibits muscle growth in a statistically significant way after about 18 months of daily use, which resembles the MASTERS trial result in older adults.[39][2]

On looksmax.org, a thread titled 'Why metformin sucks' collects claims that metformin causes B12 deficiency, neuropathy and mitochondrial problems and blunts muscle growth, and begins by saying the drug is touted in bodybuilding circles for improved insulin sensitivity and muscle building.[42] Another thread about the actor Jared Leto's youthful look speculates that he uses berberine, metformin and niagen, and posters respond with comments about his appearance.[43] These are forum opinions, not controlled data.

Wikipedia reports that in December 2019 the FDA announced that some metformin made outside the US might contain the probable carcinogen NDMA. Recalls followed in 2020 in Canada and the US, with the FDA asking five companies in May 2020 to recall sustained-release products, and revised nitrosamine guidance issued in September 2024.[1]

Metformin is prescription-only in the US, Canada, UK, EU and Australia.[1] Some T Nation posts describe obtaining it from overseas pharmacies without a prescription,[4][5] while the US label for a metformin combination product carries a boxed warning for lactic acidosis and lists severe renal impairment as a contraindication.[31][1]

lore.intro: On T Nation, metformin comes up as a diabetes drug taken by members, as an add-on to testosterone or growth hormone use, and in debates about whether it limits muscle growth; on looksmax.org it appears in a critical thread and in speculation about celebrity ageing.[39][40][4][42][43]

timeline.event: Emil Werner and James Bell first describe metformin in the scientific literature.[1]
Slotta and Tschesche report blood-sugar-lowering in rabbits, a finding largely ignored at the time.[1]
Jean Sterne tests metformin in humans, names it Glucophage, and it is introduced in France.[1]
US FDA approval for type 2 diabetes; Glucophage launches in the US on 3 March 1995.[1]
UKPDS 34 reports on metformin in overweight type 2 diabetes patients.[11]
Diabetes Prevention Program reports reduced diabetes incidence with metformin or lifestyle intervention.[7]
A mouse study reports extended healthspan and lifespan with low-concentration dietary metformin.[2]
Bannister and colleagues report survival comparisons between metformin-treated diabetics and non-diabetic controls.[2]
Barzilai and colleagues propose the TAME trial in Cell Metabolism.[2]
Randomised trials in older adults report blunted exercise adaptations (Konopka) and blunted muscle hypertrophy (MASTERS).[2]
NDMA impurity findings lead to metformin recalls in the US and Canada.[1]
A review describes emerging uncertainty about metformin's anti-ageing potential.[8]
